title: Khuyến khích sinh con · Agree / Disagree
prompt: Some people believe that paying families to have more children should be a priority. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Nêu rõ mức đồng ý với thứ tự ưu tiên trong đề; điều kiện trong thesis phải thực sự giới hạn chính sách, không chỉ nói chung cần thận trọng. Đây là gỡ rào cản, không tạo mong muốn sinh con cho mọi người. Giới hạn: Không đồng nhất tiền thưởng sinh một lần với trợ cấp chăm trẻ dài hạn. Chi phí nhà ở, thời gian và phân công chăm sóc tồn tại nhiều năm, nên chỉ tăng tiền lúc sinh có thể không đổi quyết định.

paragraphs: Payments for having children appeal to families facing insecure incomes, but raising a child requires years of money, time and dependable care rather than initial purchases alone. I support continuing financial help for families, but oppose making birth bonuses a priority ahead of reliable childcare and workable parental schedules.

Financial support can reduce some immediate costs of parenthood. Predictable assistance may reassure people whose family plans are constrained by insecure income. A regular childcare subsidy could make a second child more affordable. Because parenthood creates recurring commitments, confidence in support next year may influence family plans more than a larger sum available only at the birth. A one-off birth payment may cover initial purchases, but it does little to resolve years of childcare costs or incompatible working schedules.

One-off payments cannot resolve long working hours, housing insecurity or unequal caring duties. A parent whose shift ends after the local nursery closes may have to reduce paid hours, losing income every month despite receiving a birth bonus. If parents cannot combine work with dependable childcare, a temporary cash incentive does little to change the constraint shaping their family plans. Reliable services and flexible leave address time as well as money, recognising that a family can afford initial purchases while still lacking a workable caring arrangement. Support should be evaluated by whether families can realise their own plans without financial insecurity, rather than by treating a higher birth count as its sole measure.
Family policy works best when assistance lasts as long as the pressures it addresses; temporary rewards cannot substitute for the care and time needed to raise children.
